title: The lamp in a windless place
hookLine: the Gita's picture of a settled mind is a flame that doesn't flicker
carry: the settled mind: a lamp out of the wind
last: ASANA — A CLEAN PLACE, A FIRM SEAT.

lines: A LAMP BY AN OPEN WINDOW.
cards: Light a small oil lamp, a diya, the kind lit at a home shrine, and set it by an open window. Watch it. The flame bends, leans, jumps, nearly goes out, flares back.
Every breath of air pushes it around. Now carry it into an inner room and shut the door. The flame straightens.
It stands tall and still, so still it almost looks painted. Same lamp. Same oil.
The only difference is the wind. The Gita, chapter six, uses that picture for the mind.

teach.h: A LAMP THAT DOES NOT FLICKER.
teach.b: Verse nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, that is the picture of the yogi whose mind is held, practicing union with the self. The Sanskrit is simple: dipa, the lamp; nivata, where there's no wind.
Notice the lamp is still burning. A settled mind hasn't gone out. It's fully lit, just not being pushed around.
That's the Hindu teaching of yoga in one picture: not an empty mind, a steady one, resting in the self. Then the verses say what that stillness opens onto.
Where the mind comes to rest, seeing the self by the self, a person is content in the self. They know a joy beyond the senses, and once settled there, even heavy sorrow doesn't shake them.
Then a definition I like a lot, from verse twenty-three: yoga is the unhooking from union with sorrow. Yoga is often heard as joining. Here it's also an unjoining.
Now the practical part. Verse twenty-five: little by little, let the mind grow still.

Shanaih shanaih: slowly, slowly. And verse twenty-six gives the method in one sentence: wherever the restless mind wanders off, draw it back from there and bring it under the self. Not never wandering.

teach.h: THE LAMP IN A WINDLESS PLACE.
teach.b: Coming back. Your day is an open window: every buzz, every tab, a gust. You won't stop the wind.
Notice the lean, and shut the door again.

how: Hindus often light a lamp (diya) at the home shrine morning or evening, and some meditate by gazing at a steady flame; Gita 6.19's windless lamp is a classic image of the settled mind.

o: a small lamp with a flame

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: wherever it wanders, bring it back

s: the still flame in 6.19 means a mind that has gone out
the lamp is still burning; it's fully lit, just not being pushed around.
verse 23 defines yoga as unhooking from sorrow
yoga is the unjoining from union with sorrow.
the Gita expects a meditator's mind never to wander
verse 26 assumes it will, and says: wherever it wanders, bring it back.

games.q: you're sitting, and your mind wanders off for the tenth time. what does verse 26 tell you to do?
o: stop; you're not cut out for this.
draw it back, from wherever it went.
follow the thought to see where it goes.
games.why: draw it back. the Gita's method is the returning, slowly, slowly, as often as it takes.

practice: If you can, light a candle or a small lamp and set it where the air is still; if not, picture one just in front of you. Watch the flame.

Each time a thought blows in, notice the mind lean, then gently bring it back to the flame, without being annoyed at the wind. Verse twenty-six expects it: the practice is the returning, slowly, slowly, as many times as it takes.

wordCard.voice: Dipa. Lamp. Gita six, nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, so is the settled mind, fully lit and still.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dipa, lamp; the same root as diya and Diwali (dipavali, a row of lamps).

carryVoice: Your line: the settled mind, a lamp out of the wind. Fully lit, and not pushed around. Day one hundred eighty, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.25–6.26 (slowly, slowly; bring it back)
